stem: The student wants to provide an example of an influent stream. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Hydrologists classify streams by the direction water moves between a channel and the groundwater beneath it.
- In an effluent stream, groundwater seeps up into the channel, so flow can continue through dry spells.
- In a losing stream, water seeps down through the streambed into the aquifer below.
- Losing streams are also known as influent streams.
- Sandoval Wash, in an arid basin, carries less water downstream as flow seeps through its gravelly bed.
- Marrow Brook, in a humid valley, is fed by groundwater springs year-round.
choices: Fed by groundwater springs year-round, Marrow Brook is an example of a stream that receives water from the aquifer beneath its channel.
Influent streams, which are also known as losing streams, lose water as it seeps down through their beds into the aquifer below.
Sandoval Wash, which carries less water downstream as flow seeps through its gravelly bed into the aquifer, is a losing stream.
Unlike Marrow Brook, which is fed by groundwater springs, Sandoval Wash lies in an arid basin and has a gravelly streambed.
explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named stream tied to the property 'influent.' The notes use that word only once, to say that losing streams are also called influent streams. So any choice that names a specific stream and shows it is a losing stream gives an example of an influent stream, even if the word 'influent' never appears. Choice C names Sandoval Wash, says its water seeps through its bed into the aquifer, and calls it a losing stream. That is a specific instance clearly linked to the right category.

A.why: You correctly looked for a named stream, but you read 'influent' as 'water flowing in.' The notes define influent streams as losing streams, which send water down into the aquifer. Marrow Brook receives groundwater, which makes it an effluent stream, the opposite category.

B.why: You picked a sentence at the wrong level. It accurately defines influent streams as a category but never names a specific stream, so it gives a generalization instead of an example.

D.why: You chose the right stream but missed that the sentence never links it to the property. It compares Sandoval Wash's setting and streambed with Marrow Brook's but never says that Sandoval Wash loses water to the aquifer, so it never shows that the stream is influent.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about legume cover crops. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Cover crops are planted between cash-crop seasons to protect and enrich soil.
- Legumes, a plant family that includes clovers and vetches, host bacteria in root nodules that convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use.
- When legume cover crops are tilled under, that nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.
- Crimson clover, a legume cover crop, grows quickly in mild autumns.
- Hairy vetch, another legume cover crop, can survive winters as cold as −30°C.
- Cereal rye, a non-legume cover crop, adds no new nitrogen but absorbs leftover nitrogen that would otherwise wash away.
choices: Crimson clover and hairy vetch are both legume cover crops, though hairy vetch can survive far colder winters than crimson clover can.
Legume cover crops can survive winters as cold as −30°C, so they can protect soil even in regions with the harshest climates.
Cover crops, which are planted between cash-crop seasons, add nitrogen to the soil that becomes available to the next crop when tilled under.
Legume cover crops enrich soil for the next crop: bacteria in their root nodules capture atmospheric nitrogen, which is released when the plants are tilled under.
explanation: A generalization must make a claim about the whole category, legume cover crops, and that claim must hold for every member the notes describe. The notes give two category-level facts: legumes host nitrogen-converting bacteria in their root nodules, and legume cover crops release that nitrogen to the next crop when they are tilled under. Choice D combines exactly those facts and keeps the plural category noun as its subject. It does not stretch a fact about one member into a claim about the whole group, and it does not slip into the larger category of all cover crops.

A.why: You picked a sentence at the wrong level. It names two specific legume cover crops and compares them, so it is about individual instances, not a claim about legume cover crops as a group.

B.why: You noticed that a generalization needs a broad subject, but this one takes a fact about a single crop and applies it to the whole group. The notes say only that hairy vetch survives −30°C. They say crimson clover grows in mild autumns, so cold hardiness is not a property of all legume cover crops.

C.why: You chose a broad claim but about the wrong category. The goal is about legume cover crops, and this sentence is about all cover crops. The claim is also false for that larger group, because the notes say cereal rye, a cover crop, adds no new nitrogen.
